name: Number Matrix
blurb: A grid of numbers with one box empty.
childIntro: Look along the rows and down the columns. Both follow a rule. What number belongs in the empty box?
howItWorks: A three by three grid of numbers with one cell blank. Patterns run both across and down, so the answer can be checked two different ways. It runs at OLSAT levels D through G and is the number version of the pattern matrix.
parentTip: The best feature of this type is that you can always check yourself. Work the answer out from the row, then work it out again from the column. If the two agree, you are right. If they disagree, one of your rules is wrong. Teach your child to do both every time.

figure.alt: A three by three grid of numbers.

questions.explanation: Every row goes up by two and every column goes up by two. Along the bottom row, six, eight, then ten. Down the last column, six, eight, then ten. Both agree.
questions.strategy: Do it twice, once along the row and once down the column. They should match.

figure.alt: A three by three grid of numbers.

questions.explanation: Across each row the rule is minus three then minus one. Down each column the rule is minus ten. Along the bottom row: fourteen, eleven, ten. Down the last column: thirty, twenty, ten. Both give ten.
questions.strategy: The row rule and the column rule can be different. Work out both.

figure.alt: A three by three grid of numbers.

questions.explanation: Across each row the numbers double. Down each column they go up by the value in the first column. Along the bottom row: three, six, twelve.
questions.strategy: Doubling across is a common rule. Check it on a finished row first.

figure.alt: A three by three grid of numbers.

questions.explanation: Across each row the rule is plus three, then minus two. Down each column the rule is plus four. Along the bottom row: thirteen, sixteen, fourteen. Down the last column: six, ten, fourteen. Both give fourteen.
questions.strategy: A row rule can go up then down. Do not assume it always rises.

figure.alt: A three by three grid of numbers.

questions.explanation: In every row the third number is the first two added together. Two plus three is five. Four plus six is ten. Six plus nine is fifteen. Check it down the last column too: five, ten, fifteen, which rises by five.
questions.strategy: Try adding the first two numbers of a row together. It is a very common matrix rule.

figure.alt: A three by three grid of numbers.

questions.explanation: Each number is the row heading times the column heading, like a times table. Nine times three is twenty-seven. Or read along the bottom row: nine, eighteen, twenty-seven, rising by nine.
questions.strategy: A number grid is often just a piece of a times table.

figure.alt: A three by three grid of numbers.

questions.explanation: Across each row the numbers halve. Forty-eight, twenty-four, twelve. Thirty-six, eighteen, nine. One hundred, fifty, twenty-five.
questions.strategy: Halving twice is the same as dividing by four. Use whichever is easier.

figure.alt: A three by three grid of numbers.

questions.explanation: Each row is that number's times table: one times, two times, three times. Thirteen times three is thirty-nine.
questions.strategy: If the second number is double the first, the third is usually triple it.

figure.alt: A three by three grid of numbers.

questions.explanation: In every row the third number is the second minus the first. Five minus two is three. Ten minus six is four. Nineteen minus twelve is seven.
questions.strategy: If a row rule is not adding or multiplying, try subtracting the first from the second.

figure.alt: A three by three grid of numbers.

questions.explanation: The whole grid is square numbers multiplied together. The bottom right cell is nine times nine, which is eighty-one. You can also read the bottom row as nine, thirty-six, eighty-one, which are three squared, six squared and nine squared.
questions.strategy: When numbers grow fast and look familiar, check whether they are squares.
